cultivar: Que She (small-leaf selection from Da Hong Pao seedlings)
processing: Medium oxidation, strip-rolled and charcoal roasted to a medium level in careful short passes, because the small, dense leaf burns more easily than Shui Xian.
harvest_season: One spring picking, late: usually mid to late May, after most Wuyi cultivars, as mature shoots with three or four small open leaves.
appearance_dry: Small, slender, tightly twisted dark strips, the finest leaf among the rock teas, with a dense sweet-floral smell.
appearance_wet: Small, narrow, thick olive leaves with red rims, pointed like a bird's tongue, unfolding slowly.
taste_profile: Concentrated and perfumed: orchid and gardenia with honey, a thick, oily body, a toasty roast underneath and a long, cooling mineral aftertaste; like a Da Hong Pao with the volume turned up.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, porcelain gaiwan. The small leaf packs densely, so use slightly less by weight than for Shui Xian and keep early steeps short; it is intense and easy to over-extract.

vintage_note: Spring harvest of the current year, picked late in May, roasted over the summer and sold from autumn with the year stated; production is small and good lots sell out quickly. Medium-roasted Que She drinks well on release and improves for a year or two; it keeps three to five years sealed and dry.
description:
Que She, sparrow's tongue, is a small-leaved Wuyi cultivar with an outsized reputation: it descends from the Da Hong Pao mother trees, yields little, sprouts late, and makes one of the most concentrated and aromatic rock teas on the mountain. Do not confuse it with the green teas of the same name from Guizhou and Jiangsu, which share only the leaf-shape nickname.

The cultivar was selected in the 1980s from seedlings raised from the seed of the Jiulongke Da Hong Pao trees, and what came out was a bush with unusually small, narrow, thick leaves and slow growth. Those small leaves are why it costs what it does: a picker gathers far less weight per hour, the plant gives a late, modest crop, and the dense leaf has to be roasted gently in several short passes so that it does not scorch.

In processing it follows the normal yancha route, mature leaf, overnight shaking to a medium oxidation, strip rolling and charcoal roasting, and the result is the Da Hong Pao profile intensified. The aroma is thick with orchid and gardenia, the body is oily, and the mineral aftertaste is long and cooling. Many Wuyi makers will tell you it is more fragrant than any pure Da Hong Pao, and after a good lot it is hard to argue.

Brew it with boiling water and a slightly lighter hand on the leaf than usual, since the small strips pack tightly; quick early steeps, then lengthen. It peaks in the third and fourth infusions and keeps giving sweetness for several more.

It is sold by the current spring harvest in small quantities, mostly by Wuyi specialists, and the price is high enough that the name gets borrowed for ordinary small-leaf tea. Look for genuinely tiny, uniform strips, a roast that smells sweet, and a seller who states the year and the garden. If it is beyond budget, Qi Dan gives a quieter taste of the same lineage.
sources_note: The 1980s selection from Da Hong Pao seedlings is the usual account from the Wuyi tea research institute; exact dates vary between sources.
